scope: All 56 Deep Orbit lessons and 65 exercises; objective mapping, task contracts, hints, reference solutions and grader logic. Diagnostic wording reviewed selectively, not a complete copyedit.
limitations: No independent reviewer or learner study.
No exhaustive proof that every valid implementation passes.
Reference-solution runs and misconception rejection measure grader behavior, not transferable learning.
Lesson prerequisites were checked against module order and explicit exercise API scaffolding; whole-course first-use terminology and rendered accessibility remain open.

objectives.text: Understand what a tensor is and how it relates to JavaScript arrays
Create tensors from regular arrays using TensorFlow.js
Identify the rank (number of dimensions) of a tensor
Manage tensor memory with dispose() and tf.tidy()

recallQuestions: What is the rank of `tf.tensor2d([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])`?
lessons.judgment: Creation, rank, float32 readback and disposal are tested. tf.tidy is introduced; general resource ownership needs later repeated-inference work.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Read and interpret tensor shapes
Predict where each value lands after a reshape (row-major order)
Recognize common shapes in ML (batches, sequences, images)

recallQuestions: If a tensor has shape `[8, 224, 224, 3]`, what does each dimension represent for a typical image batch?
lessons.judgment: Reshape order and shape values are checked. Recognition of image/sequence conventions relies on self-check recall.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Read a shape-mismatch error and identify which op it comes from
Perform element-wise tensor operations (add, multiply, subtract)
Combine tensors of different shapes using broadcasting
Understand the matmul shape rule: [m,n] × [n,p] → [m,p]
Use transpose to make shapes compatible

recallQuestions: What is the shape rule for matrix multiplication, and what do you use to fix a shape mismatch?
lessons.judgment: Arithmetic, broadcasting and matrix mixing are tested. Learners do not diagnose a supplied shape-error trace. Compatible multiplication does not prove they can explain a transpose.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Create data pipelines using tf.data
Batch data into fixed-size chunks for processing
Shuffle data to prevent ordering bias
Split data into training and validation sets

recallQuestions: What is the correct order for shuffle and batch in a tf.data pipeline, and why does the order matter?
A classifier reads one sensor row at a time. Does that make a random split safe for predicting future readings?
lessons.judgment: Lazy reads, shapes, temporal membership and repeated iteration are checked. Shuffle correctness still depends on two random batch memberships differing (A15).
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Explain how feature scaling affects neural-network training
Apply z-score normalization (zero mean, unit variance)
Apply min-max normalization (scale to 0-1 range)
Recognize when to use each normalization strategy
Feed normalized readings through a real dense neuron and read its verdict

recallQuestions: Why normalize features before training?

The challenge's z-score step subtracts a [2] tensor of column means from its [4, 2] batch of readings, and nothing throws. Which rule from lesson 3 allows that, and how does it line the two shapes up?
lessons.judgment: Both scalers and their application are checked. Choosing a scaler for a new data distribution is not graded. The preview neuron is supplied before the model-building module.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Understand the anatomy of a single neuron (inputs, weights, bias)
Implement a neuron as a weighted sum plus bias
See how Array.reduce() maps to the dot product operation
Read a weight: sign for direction, magnitude for sensitivity per unit of input

recallQuestions: What does a neuron compute, and what role do weights and bias each play?
lessons.judgment: Varying inputs, widths, bias and individual weights exercise the weighted sum. Hand calculation explains the reduction; no explanation is collected.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Understand why activation functions are necessary
Implement ReLU, and read sigmoid and tanh off their ranges
Pick the activation for a slot from the range that slot needs

recallQuestions: Why does a deep network without activation functions collapse to a linear model?
lessons.judgment: ReLU is implemented across signs and shapes. Sigmoid/tanh range selection needs a separate decision task.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Build multi-layer neural networks using tf.sequential()
Understand how layers compose like a middleware chain
Configure layer sizes (units) and activations
Count a network's parameters before you build it

recallQuestions: A dense layer's parameter count comes from two numbers. Which two, and why does only the first layer need an inputShape?
lessons.judgment: Model structure and parameter arithmetic are checked. The middleware analogy is exposition rather than assessed explanation.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Trace data flow through a neural network layer by layer
Use model.predict() to run inference
Understand input and output tensor shapes at each layer
Give a flat reading the batch axis the layer expects, which is the mismatch that killed the demo

recallQuestions: Your model expects input shape [null, 8] but you pass a tensor of shape [8]. What happens, and how do you fix it?
lessons.judgment: The grader checks batching, predict calls and returned tensors, but not a learner trace through every intermediate layer.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Build and compile a complete neural network from scratch
Understand what each compilation option controls
Verify the network by its parameter count, and read its predictions before and after training
Explain why a new layer starts with random weights and zero biases

recallQuestions: What does model.compile() actually do, and what does it NOT do?

Foundations lesson 3 gave matMul one inflexible shape rule. Apply it to the 32-unit stage printed in the summary above: what shape must its kernel be, and how does that give the 128 parameters on that row?
lessons.judgment: Compilation, snapshots and before/after prediction provenance are checked. Initialization and compile semantics still require explanations; random confidence is no longer used as proof of training (A10).
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Understand what loss functions measure and why they're essential
Implement MSE for regression (predicting a number on a continuous scale) and binary crossentropy for classification (picking which class a reading belongs to)
Interpret loss values: lower is better, zero is perfect

recallQuestions: For binary classification, why is binary cross-entropy preferred over mean squared error?
lessons.judgment: MSE, BCE logits and explicit output contracts are checked (A01). Selecting an appropriate loss for an unfamiliar task is not independently assessed.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Understand gradients as the direction of steepest ascent
Implement a single gradient descent step
Predict what a learning rate that is too high does to the loss
Read a descent trace and say why the step shrinks near the minimum

recallQuestions: Your training loss explodes after a few steps. What is the most likely cause and fix?
lessons.judgment: The update and dynamic loss gradients are exercised. Exploding loss has a recall question; competing causes are not diagnosed.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Estimate a gradient numerically and count what that costs at network scale
Understand how backpropagation works at a high level
See the connection to an error travelling back up the call stack
Use tf.variableGrads() for automatic gradient computation

recallQuestions: What does tf.variableGrads() return, and what do you do with the result?
Why is numeric gradient estimation (nudge one weight, rerun) too expensive to train with, even though it's correct?
lessons.judgment: Numerical and automatic derivatives are compared with variable-specific checks. The call-stack analogy and conceptual chain-rule explanation are not elicited.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Implement the complete training loop with model.fit()
Configure epochs, batch size, and validation split
Monitor training progress with callbacks
Read the training and validation curves together to tell a plateau from overfitting

recallQuestions: Why use mini-batches of 32 to 512 samples rather than processing the full dataset at once or one sample at a time?
lessons.judgment: A real fit and patience offset are checked. diagnose ignores training loss yet calls rising validation loss overfitting; stopping length is stochastic (A16).
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Evaluate on held-out test data and read the train-vs-test gap
Interpret accuracy, loss, and confusion matrix metrics
Compare a trained classifier with a simple baseline
Tell a validation set from a test set and know which one your decisions may touch
Use the train/validation gap as a clue, then investigate possible causes

recallQuestions: A model has 95% training accuracy and 60% test accuracy. What should you investigate before choosing a fix?
Why did module 1 assign earlier rows to training and later rows to validation before shuffling, and why are separately shuffled take() and skip() pipelines risky?
Can you reuse a detector's sensitivity and false-positive rate when anomalies become rarer, when the threshold changes, or when a new sensor changes normal readings?
lessons.judgment: Held-out evaluation and score provenance are checked. Confusion matrices, baseline choice and investigation are partly covered by the ungraded build-triage transfer report, not by this grader (A17/A24).
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Understand the advantages of browser-based ML inference (privacy, latency, offline)
Identify the constraints of running models in the browser (memory, compute, cold start)
Decide between browser and server inference using the CSR-vs-SSR mental model

recallQuestions: What is the main tradeoff when moving ML inference from server to browser?
lessons.judgment: The decision function now preserves hard requirements (A02). It applies a stated policy; it does not measure hardware or network performance.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Install and import TensorFlow.js in a web project
Understand TF.js backends (WebGPU, WebGL, WASM, CPU) and their performance characteristics
Initialize TF.js, verify the active backend, and configure the right one for your target

recallQuestions: Why does the selected backend matter, and how do you check it?
lessons.judgment: Awaiting initialization and reporting the active runtime are tested. Package installation and backend performance comparisons are not performed by the grader.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Load a pre-trained TensorFlow.js model from a URL
Understand the model format: model.json manifest + weight .bin shards
Export a trained model to that pair with model.save(), in Node and in the browser
Cache models in IndexedDB for offline access and faster subsequent loads
Handle loading states and errors gracefully in the UI

recallQuestions: What does tf.loadLayersModel() return compared with fetch(url).then(r => r.json())?
lessons.judgment: One loader call and returned architecture are checked. The loader is a harness stand-in; offline cache, UI errors and real manifests are not verified here (A23). Export is practised later in export-model-artifact.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Build a real-time inference pipeline: input → preprocess → predict → display
Use tf.tidy() for automatic tensor cleanup, preventing GPU memory leaks
Preprocess raw input data to match model training format
Measure and optimize inference latency for real-time requirements
Investigate tensor growth and estimate headroom when that growth continues

recallQuestions: How do you keep repeated inference from accumulating tensors, and how do you check it?
numTensors rises from 400 at 03:00 to 1,000 at 05:00. With a budget of 10,000, what can you conclude?
lessons.judgment: Preprocessing, threshold boundaries, repeated cleanup and endpoint headroom are exercised. Latency optimization itself is deferred to profiling; the first broad objective is only partly represented by classify, which has no display UI.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Understand ONNX as a universal model interchange format
Load and run ONNX models in the browser with onnxruntime-web
Benchmark TF.js against ONNX Runtime Web on one shared backend, so the result is about the runtimes
Pick a backend from model size: where per-call overhead outweighs the arithmetic, and where it stops

recallQuestions: The 673-parameter classifier runs faster on WASM than on WebGL. Does that make WASM the faster backend?
ONNX is marketed as 'train anywhere, run anywhere'. What is the real constraint that limits that guarantee?
lessons.judgment: Real TFJS and a stand-in ONNX session test feed parity and timing placement. A device benchmark and the operator-support decision are not graded (A23).
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Understand when to reach for Transformers.js vs TFJS or ONNX Runtime
Use `pipeline()` to run pretrained models in the browser
Know which tasks have ready-made pipelines (sentiment, NER, translation, summarization, image classification, automatic speech recognition)
Reason about the bandwidth + latency cost of shipping pretrained models client-side

recallQuestions: When should you reach for Transformers.js instead of training your own model with TF.js?

Module 3 scored DEEP SCAN on a held-out slice. This pipeline arrived pretrained, with no accuracy number for the crew's reports. What has to be true of the twenty reports you label by hand before Mirza sees any of this?
lessons.judgment: Task choice, positional pairing, sorting and one load/batch are tested with an injected factory. No actual pretrained download or labeled-report evaluation runs (A23).
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Understand that every signal has two representations, the time domain and the frequency domain, and that each one hides what the other makes obvious
Identify what each domain reveals: time shows when things happen, frequency shows what repeats
Recognize why some patterns are invisible in time but obvious in frequency

recallQuestions: A capture holds a tiny periodic component underneath four louder tones. Why does looking at the frequency domain reveal it when the time domain does not?
lessons.judgment: Two actual transforms and changing captures test time similarity versus spectral differences. An explanation of why one view reveals the tone is not collected.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Understand the Fourier Transform as signal decomposition into frequency components
Compute the FFT of a signal using TensorFlow.js spectral operations
Interpret FFT output: frequency bins, magnitudes, and the Nyquist frequency

recallQuestions: Given an FFT of 128 samples taken at 128 Hz, what frequency does bin 20 correspond to, and what does a 73.4 Hz tone in that same capture read as?
lessons.judgment: Dominant bins, DC exclusion, sample rate and resolution are exercised. Nyquist/aliasing is recall only, and the nearest-bin wording overgeneralizes (A22).
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Understand spectrograms as time-frequency representations of signals
Implement the Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) by slicing a window across the signal and computing one FFT per position (the taper comes in lesson 5)
Read spectrogram output: what the axes and values mean
Connect spectrogram visualization to the DevTools waterfall mental model

recallQuestions: If you increase the STFT window size, what happens to frequency resolution and time resolution, and why can't you improve both at once?
lessons.judgment: Multiple frames, hop, burst and changing tones are tested. Reading plot axes and the waterfall analogy are not independently assessed.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Understand feature engineering as deriving useful model inputs from raw data
Convert a hertz band into fixed FFT bins and use their magnitudes as model features
Combine raw features with frequency-domain features into one vector a model can train on, and know why the FFT columns have to be normalized before training
Read why a held-out score differs from the training and validation numbers, and why re-labelling the archive moved a score without touching the model

recallQuestions: The FFT computes nothing the samples did not already hold. Why does feeding its magnitudes to the model still raise accuracy?
lessons.judgment: Feature positions and frequency bands are exercised, with a corrected exact-zero convention (A09). Set-wide scaling and explanations of score/label changes are not graded here.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Explain how cutting a finite signal spreads a tone across FFT bins
Apply windowing functions (Hann, Hamming) to taper signal edges before FFT
Explain how overlapping windows improve coverage of samples near frame edges
Choose the right window function based on the frequency resolution vs leakage tradeoff

recallQuestions: Why apply a Hann window before computing the FFT?

Your spectrogram rows now come from windows with 50% overlap, so each sample appears in two of them. Which condition from the module 1 train/validation split decides whether rows like these can be split at random, and what does the overlap do to it?
lessons.judgment: Hann weights and application are checked. Hamming selection and overlap coverage are explained; the leakage probe sums magnitudes while calling them energy (A22).
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Understand why order matters in sequential data: shuffling destroys information
Recognize why scoring one reading at a time hides temporal patterns
Prepare sequential input by creating time-step windows from a stream of readings

recallQuestions: You feed a feedforward network three readings one at a time: [0.5, 0.3, 0.7], then [0.8, 0.5, 0.9], then [0.4, 0.6, 0.1]. You run them again in reverse order. What changes about the three scores, and what does not?
lessons.judgment: Window/target alignment and rank-3 stacking are exercised. The reason single-reading inference hides temporal structure is mainly recall.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Understand the RNN as a learned reducer: (prevState, input) → newState
Build a simple RNN using TensorFlow.js layers API
Recognize the vanishing gradient problem: why simple RNNs struggle with long sequences
Read a layer's learned weights off the model and check your own arithmetic against what the layer computes

recallQuestions: A simple RNN trains on long windows, but the dependency it must learn spans dozens of time steps. After many epochs the loss is stuck at 0.693. What is happening, and what fixes it?
lessons.judgment: Manual recurrence, real layer weights, state reset, order effects and gradient products are compared. API and packed weights are explained in the task.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Understand the three LSTM gates: forget (discard), input (add), output (expose)
Build an LSTM cell with tf.layers.lstm and read its three gates and candidate out of the kernels and bias the library packs them into
Compare LSTM and GRU architectures: tradeoffs between complexity and performance
Trace the gradient backward along the cell state and say what the forget gate does to it

recallQuestions: What does the LSTM forget gate actually output, and how does that differ from a hard expiry like localStorage TTL?
The LSTM flags pulses 72 hours past the last window it trained on, yet no cell state survives between windows. What did the network actually retain?
lessons.judgment: Manual gates match a real sigmoid-gated one-unit LSTM. GRU comparison is exposition; gradient retention is explained/recalled rather than tested as a derivative.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Convert continuous signal streams into fixed-size overlapping windows
Split a stream by time before windowing it, and recognize the inflated score an every-Nth holdout produces
Pair each window with a label: the next reading when forecasting, the window's last reading when classifying
Choose a window size longer than the dependency you need to detect, and read the overlap a stride-1 window produces
Recognize the fixed-length buffer that turns a live feed into one model-ready window per reading

recallQuestions: The stride-1 pipeline scored 97.4 on a held-out fifth of the windows and 60.6 after the stream was split by time. Which score is wrong, and what produced it?
You set windowSize to 30 but the pattern you need to detect spans 50 time steps. What happens, and what should you change?
lessons.judgment: Boundary exclusion and last-reading labels are graded. Choosing a dependency-length window is recall; a live buffer is demonstrated only.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Train an LSTM for next-value prediction on time-series data
Evaluate prediction quality with MSE loss and the mean absolute error (MAE) metric
Generate multi-step forecasts by feeding predictions back as input
Convert the sensors' physical limits into the units the model works in, and clamp every fed-back reading against them

recallQuestions: The prediction model compiles with meanSquaredError, while the classifiers in earlier lessons used binaryCrossentropy. Why the switch?

The rolling forecast builds a window tensor and gets a prediction tensor back on each of its 47 steps. The module-4 inference loop wrapped that same pair in tf.tidy(). What happens to those two tensors when the callback returns, and what gets out?
lessons.judgment: Real training, model/history agreement, rolling inputs, unit conversion and disposal are exercised. MAE is logged but its interpretation and held-out forecast quality are not graded (A18).
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Understand anomaly detection as modeling normality rather than cataloging every possible anomaly
Compute a baseline mean and standard deviation from known-good readings
Flag readings with a z-score gate, and recompute the baseline when the world underneath it moves
Recognize the precision and recall tradeoff a threshold sets, and why no single cutoff satisfies both

recallQuestions: A z-score threshold of |z| > 3 flags 0.27% of samples in normal Gaussian data. If a monitor processes 100,000 readings per hour and the data is normal, roughly how many false-alarm flags does it generate per hour?
lessons.judgment: Z-score arithmetic, baseline statistics and volume projections are exercised. The incident now recommends investigation rather than declaring drift (A03). Precision/recall tradeoffs appear later.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Understand the autoencoder architecture: encoder → bottleneck → decoder
Build an autoencoder in TensorFlow.js and fit it on a training set you screened yourself
See what a contaminated training set costs: the grader runs the same code on unscreened rows and puts the two detectors side by side
Explain why reconstruction error can miss an anomaly or flag a normal input

recallQuestions: Can an autoencoder trained only on normal data reconstruct an anomaly well?
lessons.judgment: Architecture and screened fitting are exercised; contamination comparison uses two separately initialized models and hard outcome ratios (A18). Tests also wrongly say a linear autoencoder is not an autoencoder (A18).
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Compute reconstruction error as the difference between input and autoencoder output
Use MSE (mean squared error) as the anomaly score for each sample
Release the tensors a per-reading score allocates, so a detector running on every reading does not leak
Rank each feature's error against that feature's own normal error to find which dimension carries the anomaly

recallQuestions: MSE reconstruction error gives you a single scalar per sample. What does that scalar tell you, and what does it not tell you?
lessons.judgment: MSE, input/output pairing and cleanup are checked; feature ratios now describe discrepancies without prescribing retraining (A04).
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Read a percentile as a false-alarm rate, and multiply it by the reading volume to get the alert count a human sees
Understand the precision-recall tradeoff and how threshold affects each
Compare F1 maximization with an explicit false-alarm and miss cost
Choose an investigation priority from an alert-storm runbook without treating it as a confirmed cause

recallQuestions: What does F1 score measure, and why is it useful when comparing anomaly detection thresholds?
Two deployments run the same detector on the same errors: one gates the capture pipeline, the other pages the bridge crew. Why should their thresholds differ when F1 peaks at the same cutoff?
The archive records one reading per 33-second window. How many flags a week does a cutoff at the 99th percentile of normal error produce, and what does that say about percentile thresholds?
lessons.judgment: F1 candidate ranking is graded; the cost contrast is checked with a counterexample and recall, not a learner cost-minimization function. Incident triage is now explicit about uncertainty (A05).
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Combine several detection methods into an ensemble so one detector's blind spot cannot decide the verdict
Derive the statistical check yourself, and fold the autoencoder's and the LSTM's scores in beside it
Interpret ensemble agreement as an evidence count, not a probability: more detectors flagging means the reading failed more kinds of check
Read a 2-of-3 majority vote as an agreement level, and state what agreeing detectors can and cannot claim

recallQuestions: How does an autoencoder detect anomalies without ever being trained on labeled anomaly examples?

Module 1's normalization lesson says to keep min-max off open-ended streams, yet this lesson's statistical gate reads the amplitude min-max normalized. What makes that channel safe for min-max, and what does the same fact cost the gate at the top of its range?
lessons.judgment: Independent verdicts, tolerances and all two-vote combinations are checked. Agreement interpretation is recall. A zero-spread window still incorrectly silences the statistical vote (A20).
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Understand attention as dynamic relevance scoring: focusing on what matters
Learn the Query-Key-Value framework for computing attention weights
Compare direct access to earlier states with the sequential updates of an LSTM
Implement a simple attention mechanism in TensorFlow.js

recallQuestions: What are the three components of the Query-Key-Value framework in attention, and what does each do?
lessons.judgment: QKV arithmetic, unequal key/value widths and soft weighting are checked, including a single output feature (A07). Comparing recurrence with attention is primarily recall/exposition.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Apply attention specifically to the temporal dimension of sequential data
Read the weights back as one number per time step and name the steps that took the most of the budget
Use attention weights as a where-it-looked map, and state what they do not prove about why
Build the temporal attention path for the DEEP SCAN analyzer: score every step, softmax, then pool the window

recallQuestions: Why are temporal attention weights useful beyond improving prediction accuracy?
lessons.judgment: Position, weights, pooling and reversal are graded. Attention-as-explanation limits are recalled rather than judged in a new case. Single-feature output rank is fixed (A07).
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Train a one-step model and roll it forward into a multi-step forecast
Understand non-stationarity, when past patterns stop predicting the future
Build the two runs a drift check has to tell apart: a rollout that feeds itself, and a one-step replay re-seeded from the readings that arrived

recallQuestions: Why does multi-step forecasting become less reliable the further ahead you predict?
You run the drift check on a 100-step rollout and it reports that error has tripled. What did you actually measure?
lessons.judgment: Real fit plus two replay histories are checked. History provenance and mandatory loss/separation thresholds need deterministic probes (A18). Drift attribution remains recall.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Understand the Kalman filter as a predict-correct loop for state estimation
Implement a 1D Kalman filter that smooths a noisy timing signal
Connect Kalman filtering to the exponential moving average pattern
Smooth a drifting interval and read the lag that motivates a velocity state

recallQuestions: What does the Kalman gain control, and what happens when it is near 0 versus near 1?
You run this filter over eight readings that fall steadily, and its estimate ends up 0.44 above the last one. What in the filter's design put it there?
lessons.judgment: Exact gain/state updates and lag on a drifting fixture are tested. EMA connection is explained; model selection for a new motion pattern is not assessed.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Blend members two ways: equal shares, and shares weighted by each member's validation score
Explain when averaging cancels error and when it cannot: member mistakes have to land in different places
Read stacking as the trained version of the same blend, where a meta-model learns the shares instead of a formula setting them
Score an ensemble against its best single member, not against the average member

recallQuestions: When can averaging models help, and what does it fail to fix?
Your three-model ensemble scores MAE 0.041 and the members scored 0.052, 0.036, and 0.050. Did the ensemble help?
Why are the member errors here fractions of each channel's range instead of raw counts and radians?
lessons.judgment: Equal and weighted predictions, validation-derived weights and best-member comparison are checked. Stacking is explained without a trained meta-model task.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Understand LLMs as augmentation tools for structured analysis
Turn an untrusted reply into typed data: find the JSON inside the text, check every field the caller depends on, and throw rather than pass a half-built object on
Define the human-AI workflow: generate → review → correct → approve

recallQuestions: What workflow makes LLM-assisted analysis safe for factual output?
lessons.judgment: Parsing now checks types, allowed classes, confidence range and non-empty reasoning (A06). Human review of factual output is still a workflow explanation/recall task.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Structure prompts with role, context, data, and format instructions
Keep the reference context on a line of its own, so the model can tell the sector's known frequencies from the reading under review
Request structured output (JSON) for programmatic processing
Diagnose a vague prompt by naming which of the four parts is missing

recallQuestions: How do role, context, data and format help this prompt?
lessons.judgment: Prompt structure and fresh input interpolation are checked; sensible alternative role wording and prose restrictions now pass (A14). Diagnosing a vague prompt is not tested.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Understand RAG as retrieve → augment → generate: query data, inject into prompt, generate response
Build a signal retrieval step from text and metadata matching, capped to fit the prompt, that reports how many rows matched before the cap and whether the cap dropped any
Check structured claims against cited fields and units, and explain why free-text answers still need review
Distinguish metadata filters, keyword search, and embedding search, and state what the retrieval cap leaves out

recallQuestions: A generated answer contains only numbers found in retrieved records. Has it been verified?
lessons.judgment: Retrieval filters/cap and structured claim provenance are tested. Search-method choice is explanation plus retrieval limitations, not an embedding implementation; count-integrality contract remains incomplete (A21).
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Structure report generation as section-by-section assembly rather than monolithic generation
Follow a report pipeline from template to data to generation to validation to assembly, and build the assembly step that decides what ships
Cut a section that fails its check, and record the gap instead of shipping the guess
Produce a formatted report a human can sign, with the withheld sections named rather than quietly missing

recallQuestions: What does section-by-section generation make easier to review?
lessons.judgment: The assembly stage preserves validated order and lists withheld headings. Validation arrives as a boolean; reviewing generated sections is outside this grader.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Design a multi-model pipeline with clear interfaces between stages
Orchestrate a classifier, an anomaly detector and an alert writer as stages that pass one checked verdict between them
Validate each stage's output against its contract, then decide per stage: substitute a fallback, or stop the run when there is no honest substitute
Trace one capture through the full DEEP SCAN pipeline, and see why each model needs its own preprocessing rather than one shared array

recallQuestions: What can checks between model stages catch, and what requires end-to-end evaluation?

The autoencoder's stand-in here is module 7's 3-sigma gate on the amplitude alone. Why is there a ceiling on the sigma count that feature can produce, and what should you suspect when a reading comes back above it?
lessons.judgment: Actual classifier preprocessing and injected-stage orchestration are checked; detector and alert contracts now reject invalid types (A08). Architecture design is still prescribed.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Size a model's weights from its parameter count, and know why a profiling loop has to dispose what it allocates
Benchmark inference latency with high-resolution timing, mean and tail
Identify which layers hold the parameters, and know why that is not the same as which layers hold the time
Establish baseline metrics before optimization

recallQuestions: Why should you profile a model before optimizing it?
lessons.judgment: Measured mean, parameter rows, weight bytes and cleanup are checked. Tail latency is not returned by this task; wall-clock tests can fail on a busy runner (A19).
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Understand quantization as byte reduction: float32 storage cut to uint16 or uint8
Quantize a model using TensorFlow.js conversion tools
Measure what a quantized build gets wrong instead of quoting a rule of thumb for it
Know what quantization buys in the browser (download, disk, load) and what it does not (inference speed)
Know that the quantize flags take weight-name patterns, so a pass can cover some layers and skip others

recallQuestions: What trade-off does quantization make in TensorFlow.js, and how do you decide if it is acceptable?
lessons.judgment: A simulated affine kernel pass, restored predictions and constant kernels are tested (A11). Converter CLI/package output is not exercised (A23).
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Understand pruning as tree-shaking for neural networks: zero the near-zero weights
Implement magnitude-based pruning with a configurable sparsity level
Measure what each pruning level costs, one class at a time
Separate what pruning changes on disk from what it changes on the wire

recallQuestions: You zero 60% of a model's weights with magnitude pruning and re-export it with the TensorFlow.js converter. Why is the weight file the same size as before?
Pruning hurt the rare class in this experiment. Does that prove rare patterns are stored in small weights?
lessons.judgment: Global ranking, per-class effects and weight restoration are checked. Disk/wire behavior is recall. Exact sparsity 1 and unrepresented classes need an explicit contract (A21).
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Wrap a model in a cache-first predict that skips inference on a hit
Hash model inputs for cache key generation
Choose cache strategies: exact match, approximate match, TTL-based expiry, and invalidation when the model version changes
Measure cache hit rate and its impact on effective inference latency

recallQuestions: What should you measure before adding an inference cache, and why can a fresh entry be wrong?
lessons.judgment: Value keys, hits, tensor disposal and separate model caches are tested. TTL/version is covered by the incident, but an integrated bounded cache and latency tradeoff are not (A21).
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Understand WebGPU as compute-oriented GPU access (vs WebGL's graphics orientation)
Configure TensorFlow.js to use the WebGPU backend
Benchmark WebGPU vs WebGL vs WASM for inference workloads
Handle WebGPU availability with graceful fallback to WebGL

recallQuestions: Why can WebGPU help compute-heavy inference, and why should you still benchmark it?

Demir's first WebGPU timing run printed 0.4 ms and was wrong. Which rule from module 4's backend benchmark does that run break, and would disposing the output tensor before stopping the clock have fixed it?
lessons.judgment: Preference order, false/throw failures and fallback are checked with a runtime stand-in. Device performance is not measured (A23).
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Design a production ML pipeline as a dependency graph of typed components
Define interfaces between pipeline stages: preprocessor, feature extractor, classifier, reporter
Implement a pipeline runner that validates data flow between stages
Map the complete DEEP SCAN architecture from raw signal to final report

recallQuestions: Why do ML pipeline stage dependencies differ from npm package dependencies?
lessons.judgment: A supplied linear chain tests stage validation and async sequencing with real FFT/tensors. Learners do not design a dependency graph.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Extend a standard CI/CD pipeline with ML-specific validation steps
Implement model accuracy gates that block deployment on regression
Add inference performance benchmarks as CI checks
Configure automated deployment with rollback on failure
Export a model with model.save() and an in-memory save handler, and read its topology, weight specs, and byte count

recallQuestions: Why does a passing CI workflow not guarantee you tested the model you are about to ship?
What do ML model gates add to a standard web CI pipeline, and what do they share with failing unit tests?
lessons.judgment: Accuracy gating and actual in-memory export/reload are checked (A12). A runnable CI workflow, performance gate and deployed rollback are not assessed by these tasks (A23).
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Implement prediction quality monitoring: confidence tracking and the prediction-side class mix
Build latency monitoring with P50/P95/P99 percentile tracking
Detect data drift by comparing input feature distributions over time
Configure alerts that trigger when model health metrics cross thresholds

recallQuestions: What category of model failure does standard app monitoring miss entirely?
A drift alert fires in production. Why can you not settle it by reading the model's live accuracy?
lessons.judgment: Confidence mean, latency order statistics and feature-mean distance are graded. Class mix, higher-moment drift, alerts and the no-traffic state remain outside or simplified (A21).
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Write a Model Card documenting model purpose, training data, and performance
Document the pipeline API and write runbooks for common operational scenarios
List known limitations and failure modes: what the model cannot do

recallQuestions: Why does documentation discipline transfer from software to ML, but verifiability does not?
lessons.judgment: Metadata is rendered and weakest recall is derived. The learner does not author the data provenance, intended use, API docs or operational runbook.
lessons.prerequisiteReview: Read with the module sequence and explicit task scaffolding; learner readiness unvalidated.

objectives.text: Configure a production build that includes model assets alongside web assets
Deploy an ML-powered web app to GitHub Pages as a static site
Verify the deployed system loads and runs inference correctly
Rehearse the whole chain before the deploy: preprocess the archive, train the candidate, score a canary set, gate the launch
Complete the DEEP SCAN mission: classify the anomalous signal

recallQuestions: How does rolling back a deployed model differ from rolling back a deployed web app?
DEEP SCAN's final verdict fires on a 2-of-3 detector majority, the vote from module 7. That module said the majority is not three odds multiplied. What makes the three votes fail together?
lessons.judgment: Training, canary scores, cleanup, verifier sequence and finale voting are exercised. There is no learner-owned deployed project under this grader (A23/A24); the empty-pattern check is fixed (A13).
